questions.q: What is the ML platform team's product, as distinct from the data scientist's?
options: The trained models themselves
The shared tooling data scientists use to build, train, and ship models repeatably
The company's cloud billing account
The business metric the model is trying to improve
questions.explain: The ML platform team's customer is the data scientist, and its product is the shared, reusable tooling — not the models themselves, which data scientists build.

questions.q: How does an ML platform team's scope typically differ from a general infrastructure/DevOps team's scope?
options: The platform team provisions raw Kubernetes clusters from scratch
The platform team consumes infrastructure the DevOps team provides, and builds ML-specific tooling on top of it
There is no difference; they are the same team by definition
The platform team owns IAM and cloud networking directly
questions.explain: The ML platform team typically sits above general infrastructure, consuming compute/networking/IAM that an infra or DevOps team owns, and building ML-specific systems like feature stores and registries on top.

questions.q: What does "paved road" mean in this context?
options: A literal CI/CD deployment pipeline diagram
A supported, opinionated default workflow that is easier to follow than to work around
A one-time migration project to a new cloud provider
A rule that forbids any custom tooling under any circumstances
questions.explain: A paved road is a supported, opinionated way of doing something that is the path of least resistance — not a ban on customization, but a strong, easy-to-follow default.

questions.q: A platform team ships a feature store, but a data scientist must still file a ticket and wait for a platform engineer to manually register every new feature. What's missing?
options: A monitoring dashboard
A model registry
Self-service — the scientist can't complete the workflow without someone else acting on their behalf
GPU quota
questions.explain: Self-service is one of the three traits of a working paved road. If a human still has to manually complete a step, the workflow isn't self-service yet, even if the underlying tool exists.

questions.q: Why do ML platform teams typically get created, according to this lesson?
options: As a speculative investment before any model reaches production
Because leadership becomes aware of visible pain — duplicated plumbing, inconsistent standards, and slow, unpredictable time-to-production
Because a vendor requires it as a condition of a software license
To replace the data science team entirely
questions.explain: Platform teams are usually funded reactively, once the cost of not having shared tooling — duplicated work, inconsistent standards, slow shipping — becomes visible and painful enough to justify the investment.
